title: My Adidas
hook: A rap group wrote a song about their trainers, and Adidas signed them.
situation: Run-DMC wore Adidas Superstars without laces as part of their look, and released a single called ‘My Adidas’ in 1986. Sportswear brands signed athletes, not musicians.
exchange: Adidas signed the group to an endorsement deal. Run-DMC gave Adidas a place in hip-hop culture that no advertising could have bought.
brought: Money, product and a global sportswear brand.
A hit song, a look and credibility with a new generation.
turning_point: At a Madison Square Garden concert, an Adidas executive watched thousands of fans hold their trainers in the air as the group performed the song. The deal followed.
metric_label: The deal, per Guinness World Records
measure: The value Guinness gives for the first sneaker deal with people outside sport. Other sources say $1m
evidence: The deal is recorded as the first sneaker endorsement for non-athletes, but its value and year vary between sources. No sales effect was published.
lesson: The best cultural partners are already using your product. Find the people who chose you before you paid them.
take: Adidas didn’t create the moment. It saw it in a crowd at Madison Square Garden and had the sense to back it.

creative.label: Watch the 1986 Adidas USA promo preserved by The Hip Hop Museum
creative.heading: Partnership media

announcement: See the record · Guinness World Records
deal_value: $1.6m according to Guinness World Records, $1m in other accounts
how_to_measure: For Adidas, track sales of the shoe in the cities where the group was strongest, before and after the deal. For the group, record ticket sales and album sales after the song became an anthem.

title: Since 1928
stage: Signed and renewed for a century
situation: At the 1928 Amsterdam Games, Coca-Cola was there with the American team. The Olympics were growing into the world’s biggest sporting event.
exchange: Coca-Cola has paid to be an official Olympic partner. The Games have had one of the world’s best-known brands at their side.
brought: Sponsorship money and a global marketing machine.
The world’s most watched sporting event, every two years.
turning_point: In 2019 the partnership was extended to 2032, jointly with the Chinese dairy company Mengniu. The International Olympic Committee calls Coca-Cola its longest-standing partner.
metric_label: From 1928 to the end of the current deal in 2032
measure: The length of the partnership if it runs to the end of its current term. A fact, not a result
evidence: The renewals are the evidence: Coca-Cola keeps choosing the Olympics. No public figure shows what each Games adds, and health groups have urged the IOC to end the deal.
lesson: A partnership that lasts a century becomes part of both brands. It also means you inherit each other’s criticism.
take: Nearly a hundred years in, nobody asks what the Olympics does for Coca-Cola any more. That’s the most valuable thing a partnership can earn, and the most dangerous.

creative.label: Watch Coca-Cola’s archivists look back on 90 years of Olympic sponsorship
creative.heading: Partnership media

announcement: Read about the IOC partnership · Olympics.com
impact_source: Read about the 2032 extension · Business Standard
deal_value: The 2019 joint deal with Mengniu was reported at up to $3bn, unconfirmed

image.alt: A Coca-Cola installation at the Olympic Games
image.credit: Coca-Cola Olympic activation · International Olympic Committee

how_to_measure: After a long partnership, the question is what each Games still adds. Compare sales and brand preference in each host country with similar countries during Games years, and track how many people still link the brand to the Olympics.

title: The Choice of a New Generation
hook: The biggest pop star in the world rewrote ‘Billie Jean’ for a soft drink.
situation: Pepsi was fighting Coca-Cola for younger drinkers. Michael Jackson had just released Thriller, the best-selling album of the era.
exchange: Pepsi paid Jackson and his brothers a record fee. Jackson reworked ‘Billie Jean’ into a Pepsi jingle for the ‘new generation’ campaign.
brought: A record endorsement fee and a huge advertising budget.
The most famous voice in the world and a generation of fans.
turning_point: The campaign ran in 1984. During filming, Jackson’s hair caught fire, and the accident became part of the story.
metric_label: The reported fee, then a record
measure: The reported value of the 1984 deal. A second deal in the late 1980s was reported at $10m
evidence: Pepsi’s sales reached $7.7bn in 1984 and its share rose while Coca-Cola’s fell, according to reports at the time. Those figures sit alongside the campaign, and no source separates its effect.
lesson: When a partner is the culture of the moment, the deal can change the category, not just your share of it.
take: The deal that set the price of celebrity in advertising for a generation. It made the endorsement fee a headline in itself.

creative.label: Watch Michael Jackson and the Jacksons in Bob Giraldi’s Pepsi Generation advert
creative.heading: Partnership media

deal_value: Reported at about $5m, a record for a celebrity endorsement at the time

image.alt: A young Alfonso Ribeiro drinks Pepsi in the 1984 advert
image.credit: Pepsi Generation (1984) · still from director Bob Giraldi’s archive

how_to_measure: Compare Pepsi’s share in the weeks the adverts ran with weeks without them, region by region, to separate the campaign from the wider trend. For Jackson, track album sales and concert demand around the launch.

title: Absolut Warhol
hook: A vodka bottle became a work of art, and then an art collection.
situation: Absolut was building a brand in America around its distinctive bottle. Andy Warhol was the most famous artist in the world.
exchange: Absolut commissioned Warhol to paint its bottle. Warhol made two paintings, and one became an advert.
brought: A commission and a bottle shape worth painting.
The name that made art and advertising the same thing.
turning_point: The 1985 painting started a tradition: between 1985 and 2004 Absolut commissioned 850 works from 550 artists for its advertising.
measure: The size of the Absolut Art Collection that grew from Warhol’s commission. A fact, not a result
evidence: The collection and its use in advertising are well documented. The second Warhol painting resurfaced in 2020 and became a limited-edition bottle, which Absolut’s owner says drove growth, without giving numbers.
lesson: One great collaboration can become a platform. Ask whether the first partner can open the door to many more.
take: Warhol painted a bottle, and Absolut spent twenty years turning that into its whole identity. The partnership outlived the man.

creative.label: Watch Absolut Warhol: From 1985 to Today on Absolut’s channel
creative.heading: Partnership media

impact_source: See the painting · National Galleries of Scotland

image.alt: Andy Warhol’s blue painting of an Absolut bottle
image.credit: Blue Absolut Warhol artwork · The Absolut Company press archive

how_to_measure: Track awareness and premium price acceptance in markets where the art adverts ran against markets where they didn’t. For the artists, record how many commissions led to wider recognition or gallery sales.

title: Art You Could Wear
hook: A street artist put his figures on a cheap plastic watch.
situation: Swatch had been launched in 1983 as an affordable, fashionable Swiss watch. Keith Haring wanted art to reach everyone, and opened a shop to sell it cheaply.
exchange: Haring designed watches for Swatch. Swatch put his art on people’s wrists at an affordable price.
brought: An affordable watch made in huge numbers.
Instantly recognisable art and credibility in New York culture.
turning_point: Swatch dates Haring’s watches to 1986, a year after its first artist watch by Kiki Picasso. Artist editions became a Swatch tradition.
metric_label: The year of Haring’s Swatch designs
measure: The year Swatch gives for Haring’s watches. Some collectors date the first to 1985
evidence: The watches are now collectors’ items, and Swatch has worked with many artists since. No sales figure was published.
lesson: Partner with an artist whose values match your product. Haring wanted art for everyone, and Swatch was a watch for everyone.
take: The most natural fit in this edition. Neither side had to pretend. Haring sold cheap art, and Swatch made the cheap watch desirable.

creative.label: Watch the Haas collection’s film about artist-designed Swatches, including Keith Haring
creative.heading: Partnership media

impact_source: See a Haring watch at auction · Christie’s

image.alt: Four Swatch watches designed by Keith Haring
image.credit: Keith Haring Swatch watches · Christie’s catalogue photography

how_to_measure: Report sales of each artist edition against standard designs released in the same season, and resale prices over time. For the artist, track recognition among younger buyers outside the art world.

title: Be Like Mike
hook: An advert so catchy that its song outlived the campaign.
situation: Gatorade already dominated sports drinks. Michael Jordan had just won his first championship.
exchange: Gatorade signed Jordan as its only endorser. The ‘Be Like Mike’ advert showed children dreaming of playing like him.
brought: A ten-year contract and national advertising.
The most admired athlete in America.
turning_point: The advert aired on 8 August 1991, the same day Gatorade announced the deal. Its song became a hit in its own right.
measure: The reported value of the ten-year deal. A deal term, not a result
evidence: The advert is one of the most remembered in sport. Gatorade already led its category, and a widely quoted sales jump came before the advert aired. Some accounts say it didn’t drastically change sales.
lesson: When you already lead the market, a cultural partner may defend your position rather than grow it. Measure accordingly.
take: The song is famous, the sales effect is not. It’s a reminder that the most loved adverts aren’t always the ones that moved the numbers.

creative.label: Watch the remastered 1991 Be Like Mike television advert
creative.heading: Partnership media

image.alt: Michael Jordan smiles as he drinks from a Gatorade bottle
image.credit: Be Like Mike (1991) · still from the remastered advert

how_to_measure: Gatorade already led the category, so measure share among young athletes and preference against rivals, before and after the advert, in markets where it ran heavily and markets where it didn’t.

title: Phish Food
data_source: A Vermont band, a Vermont ice cream
hook: Two Vermont institutions made an ice cream together.
situation: Phish was a Vermont band with a devoted touring following. Ben & Jerry’s was a Vermont ice cream company already known for flavours with personality.
exchange: Phish lent its name to a flavour and directed its royalties to charitable causes. Ben & Jerry’s made and sold the ice cream.
brought: Ice cream, freezers in shops and a playful brand.
A loyal fan base and local credibility.
turning_point: Phish Food launched in 1997 with a concert at the Flynn Theatre in Burlington, and is still on sale.
measure: The year of launch. A flavour still on sale decades later is a fact, not a sales figure
evidence: The flavour’s long life suggests it sells, but Ben & Jerry’s doesn’t publish sales by flavour, and claims that it is the best-seller conflict.
lesson: Local partnerships can travel. Shared roots make the story believable a long way from home.
take: The partnership works because it feels like neighbours, not a deal. That is hard to fake.

creative.label: Watch Phish’s footage from the 1997 Flynn Theatre benefit that launched Phish Food
creative.heading: Partnership media

announcement: Read the origin story · Tasting Table
impact_source: Read about pop culture flavours · Mental Floss

image.alt: An open tub of Ben & Jerry’s Phish Food ice cream
image.credit: Phish Food packaging · Ben & Jerry’s product photography

how_to_measure: Report sales of the flavour against the range average each year, and how many first-time Ben & Jerry’s buyers start with it. For the band, track donations to its charity and ticket sales in towns where the flavour sold well.

title: Monogram Multicolore
hook: An artist repainted the most famous monogram in fashion in 33 colours.
situation: Louis Vuitton’s brown monogram was iconic but serious. Its creative director, Marc Jacobs, wanted it to feel young and playful.
exchange: Takashi Murakami redrew the LV monogram in 33 colours on white and black canvas. Louis Vuitton made it into bags sold around the world.
brought: Pop art colour and a cult following in Japan and the art world.
turning_point: The Multicolore line launched for spring and summer 2003 and became one of the defining bags of the decade.
measure: A figure repeated in many accounts. Another, attributed to WWD, put 2003 sales at $345m, about 10% of the brand
evidence: The sales figures are widely repeated but traced to secondary sources rather than LVMH’s accounts. The line was discontinued in 2015.
lesson: Letting an artist play with your most sacred asset can renew it, as long as the asset stays recognisable.
take: Vuitton let an artist touch its crown jewel. The risk was enormous, and the monogram came out younger.

creative.label: Watch Takashi Murakami’s Superflat Monogram on Louis Vuitton’s channel
creative.heading: Partnership media

impact_source: Read about the sales · NSS Magazine

image.alt: An animated girl against a purple Louis Vuitton monogram
image.credit: Superflat Monogram (2003) · Louis Vuitton’s remastered film

how_to_measure: Report sales of the line against classic monogram sales in the same stores and seasons, and the share of new and younger customers. For Murakami, track gallery prices and exhibition demand after the launch.

title: The U2 iPod
hook: A rock band got its own iPod.
situation: Apple was making the iPod the way people carried music. U2 had a new album, and record labels were nervous about digital music.
exchange: Apple made a black and red U2 edition of the iPod and an advert with the band playing ‘Vertigo’. The single was sold exclusively through iTunes in the US.
brought: The iPod, iTunes and its silhouette adverts.
A new single and one of the biggest bands in the world.
turning_point: Announced in October 2004, the U2 iPod carried the band’s signatures on the back and came with a discount on U2’s complete catalogue on iTunes.
metric_label: How long the U2 iPod was on sale
measure: The special edition’s time on sale. A fact, not a result
evidence: No sales figures for the special edition were published. The partnership is remembered for the advert and the iTunes tie-in, and a decade later the same partners made a much less popular move.
lesson: When both sides bring a product, the partnership can sell each other’s. Design the deal so both products benefit.
take: The iPod advert that felt like a music video. Ten years later the same partners pushed an album onto everyone’s phones, and that’s in Failure first.
credit: Apple, U2 and Universal Music Group, 2004

creative.label: Watch Apple’s 2004 Vertigo iPod advert featuring U2
creative.heading: Partnership media

impact_source: Read the product history · Apple History

image.alt: A black silhouette of a U2 performer against a yellow background
image.credit: Vertigo (2004) · Apple television advert still from an archive upload

how_to_measure: Report special edition iPod sales against standard models in the same months, and iTunes catalogue sales for the band before and after. For the band, track album sales and streams among people new to them.

title: Adidas by Stella McCartney
stage: Launched and running for two decades
hook: A fashion designer made women’s sportswear worth wearing, and stayed.
situation: Women’s sportswear was often men’s kit made smaller. Stella McCartney, known for luxury fashion without leather, wanted to design for active women.
exchange: McCartney designed performance collections for running, gym and swimming. Adidas made and sold them worldwide.
brought: Sports science, factories and global distribution.
Fashion credibility and a design point of view.
turning_point: Announced in September 2004, the line reached shops in 2005. In 2010 Adidas made McCartney creative director for Team GB’s kit at London 2012.
metric_label: The start of a partnership still running
measure: The year of launch. Lasting two decades is a fact, not a sales figure
evidence: Neither side publishes the line’s sales. Its longevity, a dedicated store from 2012 and the Team GB role suggest both have found it worth continuing.
lesson: A designer partnership can outlast a capsule collection if the designer solves a real problem for customers.
take: Most designer collaborations last a season. This one lasted twenty years because it filled a gap, not just a headline.

creative.label: Watch Stella McCartney’s Adidas spring and summer 2020 campaign film
creative.heading: Partnership media

impact_source: Read about the first store · RetailDetail

image.alt: Models in blue sportswear in the Adidas by Stella McCartney campaign
image.credit: Adidas by Stella McCartney SS20 · still from Stella McCartney’s campaign film

how_to_measure: Report the line’s sales and full-price sell-through against Adidas women’s performance wear, and the share of buyers new to the brand. For McCartney, track awareness of her own label in markets where the line sold well.

title: The Heart on the Chuck
data_source: Comme des Garçons’ heart, Converse’s Chuck Taylor
hook: A small heart with eyes made a classic trainer fashionable again.
situation: The Chuck Taylor was a classic, but common. Comme des Garçons, the Japanese fashion house, had a playful sub-label, PLAY, with a heart logo designed by Filip Pagowski.
exchange: Comme des Garçons put its PLAY heart on Converse’s Chuck Taylor. Converse brought the shoe and the distribution.
brought: The Chuck Taylor and shops around the world.
Fashion credibility and the heart logo.
turning_point: The heart first appeared on the Chuck Taylor in 2009, with a wider release in 2015. In 2024 the partners marked fifteen years.
measure: The length of the partnership when the brands marked its anniversary. A fact, not a result
evidence: The shoe is a staple in fashion stores, and the partnership keeps being renewed. Neither brand publishes its sales.
lesson: A small mark from the right partner can change how people see a familiar product. Keep the change small and the product intact.
take: The smallest intervention in this edition, and one of the longest-lasting. Sometimes a partner only needs to add a heart.
credit: Converse and Comme des Garçons PLAY

creative.label: Watch Sean Lew’s Chuck 70 campaign film on the Comme des Garçons channel
creative.heading: Partnership media

image.alt: Cream and black Converse shoes with the red Comme des Garçons PLAY heart
image.credit: 2009 Chuck Taylor collaboration · product photography via Hypebeast

how_to_measure: Report sales and full-price sell-through against standard Chuck Taylors in the same stores. For Comme des Garçons, track how many buyers go on to its own lines, using store and online accounts where they can be linked.

title: Amy Winehouse for Fred Perry
stage: Launched and continued with her foundation
hook: A singer designed clothes for a British brand, and the partnership continued after her death.
situation: Amy Winehouse’s look drew on the British subcultures Fred Perry had long dressed. Fred Perry wanted to reach a new generation of women.
exchange: Winehouse designed womenswear collections for Fred Perry. Fred Perry made and sold them.
brought: Her style, her designs and her fans.
turning_point: Winehouse died in July 2011 with two seasons still to come. With her family’s approval, Fred Perry released them and gave her royalties and fees to the Amy Winehouse Foundation.
metric_label: Raised for the Amy Winehouse Foundation, per Fred Perry
measure: Donations reported by Fred Perry, which gives a share of the collection’s revenue to the foundation
evidence: The donations are reported by the brand, and totals vary by date. No figure shows what the collections did for Fred Perry’s own sales.
lesson: If a partnership outlives its plan, let the partner’s family and values decide what happens next.
take: The most moving case in the archive. Fred Perry found a way to carry on that honoured her rather than profited from her.

creative.label: Watch Amy Winehouse discuss her Fred Perry collection in an archive upload
creative.heading: Partnership media

announcement: Read about the decision to continue · Rolling Stone
impact_source: Read about the donations · Brands Untapped

image.alt: Amy Winehouse models a black jacket from her Fred Perry collection
image.credit: Amy Winehouse for Fred Perry, autumn and winter 2010 · campaign photography via DSCENE

how_to_measure: Report money raised for the foundation each season and publish the total in one place, since the figures vary. For Fred Perry, compare sales of the collections with its own women’s range, and track how buyers feel about the brand.

title: Magna Carta Holy Grail
hook: Samsung bought a million copies of an album before it came out.
situation: Samsung wanted its Galaxy phones to feel culturally relevant against the iPhone. Jay-Z had a new album and wanted a different way to release it.
exchange: Samsung bought a million copies of the album and gave them free to Galaxy owners through an app, three days before it reached shops.
brought: Money, and millions of Galaxy phones to deliver the album to.
A new album and one of the biggest names in music.
turning_point: The album was released to Galaxy owners on 4 July 2013. The music industry body, the RIAA, changed its rules so digital albums could be certified platinum on release day.
metric_label: Copies Samsung bought and gave away
measure: The number of copies distributed through the app. Billboard refused to count them in its charts
evidence: The million copies and the RIAA change are documented. Billboard didn’t count the copies, and Samsung published no figure for what the deal did for phone sales.
lesson: Buying a cultural moment outright can rewrite an industry’s rules. Make sure it also rewrites what customers think of you.
take: Jay-Z was paid before anyone heard a note. It was a brilliant deal for the artist, and a harder one to prove for the phone.

creative.label: Watch Oceans, a short from Samsung’s Magna Carta Holy Grail campaign
creative.heading: Partnership media

impact_source: Read about the rule change · Fact
deal_value: Reported at $5m, though other reports gave different figures

image.alt: Pharrell Williams in a Samsung campaign film for Jay-Z’s album
image.credit: Oceans · Samsung and Jay-Z campaign film still from Allison Hayes’s archive

how_to_measure: Compare Galaxy sales and app downloads among young buyers in the weeks around the release with the same weeks the year before. For the artist, report sales, streams and touring income, separately from the million copies Samsung bought.

title: Fenty Puma
hook: A pop star became a sportswear brand’s creative director, and its women’s business took off.
situation: Puma was struggling to compete with Nike and Adidas, especially with women. Rihanna was one of the most influential style figures in the world.
exchange: Puma made Rihanna creative director of its women’s line. She designed collections, including a creeper trainer that sold out.
brought: Production, distribution and a creative director role.
Design, influence and a vast young audience.
turning_point: Rihanna joined Puma in December 2014. Her Creeper sold out within hours in 2015, and the Fenty Puma line ran until 2018.
measure: Growth in Puma’s quarterly sales, which the company said Rihanna’s shoes were helping to drive in its women’s business
evidence: Puma credited Rihanna with lifting its women’s business, but women’s sportswear was growing across the industry, and Puma’s chief executive later said the company’s total revenue didn’t depend on her.
lesson: A celebrity creative director works when they design, not just endorse. Give them real authority over the product.
take: Rihanna didn’t just wear Puma, she made it. That’s the difference between an endorsement and a partnership.

creative.label: Watch Puma go behind the scenes of Rihanna’s Fenty Creeper campaign
creative.heading: Partnership media

impact_source: Read about Rihanna and Puma · Quartz

image.alt: Rihanna and a model pose in Puma’s Fenty Creeper campaign
image.credit: Fenty Puma Creeper · still from Puma’s behind-the-scenes film

how_to_measure: Report Fenty Puma sales and their share of women’s growth against the category trend for the same period. For Rihanna, track the brand’s growth under her own name and the platform it gave her later businesses.

title: The Ten
hook: A designer took apart ten of Nike’s most famous shoes, and put them back together with quotation marks.
situation: Nike had decades of classic shoes. Virgil Abloh, of the Off-White label, was the most influential designer for a young streetwear audience.
exchange: Abloh redesigned ten Nike classics, from the Air Jordan 1 to the Air Max 90, with exposed foam, labels and quotation marks.
brought: Ten of its most famous shoes and its production.
A design language a generation recognised instantly.
turning_point: ‘The Ten’ was released in 2017. Abloh later became Louis Vuitton’s menswear artistic director, and the shoes’ resale value soared.
metric_label: Average resale price of the white Air Jordan 1, per StockX data
measure: Average resale prices analysed by Highsnobiety. A demand signal, not Nike’s sales
evidence: Resale prices show huge demand, but they are made by resellers, not Nike. Nike published no sales or brand figures for the collaboration.
lesson: A designer can make your archive feel new. Watch the resale market: it tells you how much value you left on the table.
take: Abloh appeared in Edition 01 with IKEA. Here he did the same trick for Nike: he made the familiar feel rare.

creative.label: Watch Virgil Abloh discuss The Ten at Nike’s 2017 Off Campus event
creative.heading: Partnership media

image.alt: A red and white Nike Air Jordan 1 reworked by Virgil Abloh
image.credit: The Ten (2017) · Hypebeast’s Off Campus interview thumbnail

how_to_measure: Nike can’t claim resale value. Measure full-price sell-through, how many entrants joined each release, and whether buyers went on to other Nike lines. For the designer, track demand for his own label after each drop.
